In [[mathematics]], the '''Rees matrix semigroups''' are a special [[Class (set theory)|class]] of [[semigroup]]s introduced by [[David Rees (mathematician)|David Rees]] in 1940.{{sfn|Rees|1940}} They are of fundamental importance in [[semigroup theory]] because they are used to classify certain classes of [[Simple (abstract algebra)|simple]] semigroups.

== Definition ==

Let ''S'' be a semigroup, ''I'' and ''Λ'' [[Empty set|non-empty]] [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] and ''P'' a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] indexed by ''I'' and ''Λ'' with entries ''p''<sub>''λ'',''i''</sub> taken from ''S''.
Then the Rees matrix semigroup ''M''(''S''; ''I'', ''Λ''; ''P'') is the set ''I''×''S''×''Λ'' together with the product formula

:''(i, s, λ)(j, t, μ) = (i, s{{Hair space}}p<sub>λ,j</sub>&thinsp;t, μ)''.

Rees matrix semigroups are an important technique for building new semigroups out of old ones.

== Rees' theorem ==

In his 1940 paper Rees proved the following theorem characterising [[completely simple semigroup]]s: 

{{quote|A semigroup is completely simple if and only if it is [[isomorphic]] to a Rees matrix semigroup over a [[Group (mathematics)|group]].}}

That is, every completely simple semigroup is isomorphic to a semigroup of the form ''M''(''G''; ''I'', ''Λ''; ''P'') for some group ''G''. Moreover, Rees proved that if ''G'' is a group and ''G''<sup>0</sup> is the semigroup obtained from ''G'' by attaching a [[semigroup#Identity and zero| zero element]], then ''M''(''G''<sup>0</sup>; ''I'', ''Λ''; ''P'') is a [[regular semigroup]] if and only if every row and column of the matrix ''P'' contains an element that is not 0. If such an ''M''(''G''<sup>0</sup>; ''I'', ''Λ''; ''P'') is regular, then it is also [[Completely simple semigroup|completely 0-simple]].
